title: Technical deep dive: Multi-region routing & failover
summary: Deep technical session on multi-region routing, failover policies, and DR playbooks for deploying Redwood runtime in a healthcare-regulated environment. Covered policy routing (latency/cost/region), capacity considerations, KV cache behavior during failover, batching impacts, quantization tradeoffs, VPC/on-prem limitations, and suggested runbooks for failover and canary testing. Agreed next steps: share runbook, schedule benchmark, provide security docs and pricing worksheet.
topics: VPC / on-prem constraints and network egress

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-17
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Daniel Liu (Redwood Infra), Sofia Reyes (Redwood Product), Mark Turner (Crestline CTO), Lina Gomez (Platform Eng), Ravi Patel (SRE), Emily Chen (Security), Jordan Park (ML Eng)

Summary (auto): Deep dive into multi-region routing and failover design focusing on policy routing, regional capacity, KV cache behavior, batching/quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem considerations.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro - im alex, AE on redwood, and with me is priya se and daniel infra, sofia product. we'll run through the routing patterns and then deep dive into cache/failover.
[00:12] Mark Turner: thanks alex. high level goal - Crestline needs a multi-region setup for latency and compliance, plus a DR plan that doesnt break patient-data guarantees. also cost is a big deal.
[00:26] Priya Shah: great, lina and ravi, can you share the current infra? like do you run across two cloud regions now? what traffic % is EU vs US?
[00:36] Lina Gomez: yeah we have primary in us-east-1 and a DR region in eu-west-1. roughly 80% us, 18% eu, 2% APAC. peak is about 1.2k rps for the inference endpoints.
[00:47] Ravi Patel: we also have strict egress and VPC peering rules due to PHI, so any cross-region routing needs to honor data residency and KMS keys per region.
[00:57] Priya Shah: noted. so two primary concerns are latency and regulatory boundaries. i'll start with policy routing patterns we typically support: latency-based routing, cost-tier routing (cheaper quantized models), and region-affinity routing for residency.
[01:08] Priya Shah: latency-based: route to the nearest region unless capacity SLO breached; cost-tier: route to lower-cost quantized model in same region for low-pri traffic; region-affinity: force requests with residency flag to a region only.
[01:24] Jordan Park: question - how do you handle model variants during failover? like if us-east goes down, do you spin up eu model or route to a quantized fallback?
[01:34] Daniel Liu: good q. our typical playbook is: prefer warm standby models in DR region (same precision if possible). if capacity limited, we route to compatible quantized variant as fallback with a quality tag in the response. we also have automatic KV cache warming strategies to reduce cold starts.
[01:52] Mark Turner: KV cache warming - can you elaborate? our sessions are long and context windows are big, worried about cold cache penalties.
[02:03] Priya Shah: sure. KV cache is per-host and per-model; when failing over we do two things: proactive warming by preloading prefixes for high-volume users, and progressive warming where traffic is mirrored to DR region for a short window prior to switch. that reduces the tail latency.
[02:24] Ravi Patel: mirrored traffic sounds like it may violate residency unless we mask PHI. how do you manage that?
[02:31] Sofia Reyes: for PHI we recommend tokenized or pseudonymized payloads for warming; otherwise you can limit warming to non-sensitive prompts or synthetic workloads that represent typical prefix distributions. we document recommended hashes and truncation.
[02:47] Emily Chen: on encryption & KMS - if we have per-region keys, how does redwood handle key access during a failover? we cant have keys copied cross-region.
[02:57] Daniel Liu: we integrate with customer KMS in each region. failover playbook requires that DR region has its own KMS key and access policies pre-provisioned; we do not copy keys. you must pre-approve the DR principal. during failover we rotate to the DR key and audit logs indicate the key switch.
[03:14] Mark Turner: and what about KV cache consistency? if we warm prefixes but there are ephemeral state differences, could that leak context?
[03:25] Priya Shah: KV cache stores attention states theres no user-level secret stored, but yes the cache may contain recent tokens. we recommend TTLs and masking for any sensitive tokens, and clear cache on explicit failover if policy requires zero residual. normally we rely on warm-prefix approach plus progressive traffic mirroring to keep user experience intact.
[03:44] Jordan Park: performance numbers - if we route to a quantized fallback, what's the typical latency delta and quality regression?
[03:52] Daniel Liu: depends on quant level. int8 quantized models are ~1.4x faster and ~30-50% fewer GPU cycles, but some models show quality deltas in edge cases. we run evals per prompt set. for latency, expect 10-40ms improvement tail depending on sequence length and batch.
[04:12] Priya Shah: also batching affects this; larger batches amortize decoding cost but increase P95 latency. we recommend adaptive batching: smaller batch targets when latency-sensitive, larger batches in background or for cheaper routes.
[04:28] Lina Gomez: adaptive batching - is that automatic? can we set SLOs per route?
[04:34] Priya Shah: yes, you can set per-route latency SLOs and the runtime picks batching parameters. routes can be labeled e.g., gold (latency <= 120ms), silver (<= 300ms), bronze (best-effort).
[04:48] Mark Turner: what about networking overhead across regions if we keep KV cache warm by mirroring, does that add a lot of egress cost?
[04:56] Daniel Liu: it can. mirroring high throughput will incur egress. common approach is to mirror a sample or synthetic prefixes. Redwood's optimizer suggests the minimal synthetic set to achieve 90% hit-rate. we can share the sample set.
[05:10] Priya Shah: let's walk through a failover scenario: primary region (us-east) has an outage. routing policy detects SLO breach; traffic shifts to eu-west where we have warm standby. steps: 1) route update + circuit-breaker, 2) spin extra instances, 3) KV cache progressive warm, 4) fall back to quantized variant if needed, 5) notify and start DR runbook.
[05:33] Ravi Patel: about step 2 - spin extra instances - how long to get to capacity if we dont have reserved capacity in DR?
[05:40] Daniel Liu: cold spin-up on demand varies by cloud and instance type; 2-6 minutes typical for GPU, but can be slower. for critical apps we recommend reserved capacity or warm pool (baked AMIs or standby nodes) to hit under 90s.
[05:54] Mark Turner: we are leaning towards having reserved Dedicated capacity in DR region for guaranteed failover. cost tradeoff though.
[06:02] Alex Morgan: yes that maps to Dedicated option predictable throughput vs hosted spiky. we can model cost; i'll include pricing scenarios in the worksheet.
[06:12] Jordan Park: can we do partial failover per-customer or route? i.e., divert only non-sensitive traffic first?
[06:19] Priya Shah: absolutely. routes are per-API-key/route; you can mark requests with metadata (residency, sensitivity) and build routing policies. progressive failover strategy is common: start with low-sensitivity traffic and ramp.
[06:32] Ravi Patel: what about tests? we need a DR test that doesn't impact production.
[06:36] Sofia Reyes: recommended playbook: canary failover window during low-traffic, mirror 1% traffic, monitor latency/quality and KV warm hits, then increase to 10% etc. also run synthetic replay to exercise cold-starts.
[06:51] Emily Chen: one compliance point - audit logs. can you ensure all failover events, KMS switches, routing decisions are logged and retained where we need them?
[06:58] Daniel Liu: yes, console includes per-request traces, key rotation events logged, and we can export logs to your SIEM. retention is configurable as an add-on.
[07:08] Mark Turner: any gotchas with VPC and private deployments? we are exploring on-prem vs VPC options.
[07:15] Priya Shah: for private deployments, we require customer-provided network connectivity; cross-region peering can be more complex. also on-prem GPUs may differ and quantization/kernels may vary so profiling is important.
[07:28] Lina Gomez: we have air-gapped sites in some clinics; how would you handle updates and failover there?
[07:34] Daniel Liu: air-gapped on-prem needs pre-provisioned model bundles and local serving; failover in that case is regional only within the site. for cross-site failover you'd need approved secure transfer processes.
[07:46] Jordan Park: earlier you mentioned automatic fallback to quantized models - is inference deterministic across variants? we worry about hallucinations changes.
[07:55] Priya Shah: not deterministic; quantization can slightly change outputs. we suggest gating important prompts to gold routes and instrument evals with prompt sets to detect regressions. Redwood Optimize flags regressions and can trigger rollbacks.
[08:09] Mark Turner: can you walk us through a real-world DR playbook example? like step-by-step with triggers and owners.
[08:16] Daniel Liu: sure - example playbook (short):
 - Trigger: region SLO breach > 3 mins or full control-plane outage.
 - Auto step 1: Route shift to DR region for non-sensitive routes (circuit-breaker opens).
 - Auto step 2: Spin warm nodes in DR; enable progressive mirroring for 5-10 mins.
 - Manual step: Ops confirm KMS DR key active and approve region-affinity exceptions.
 - Auto step 3: If sustained capacity shortfall, route to quantized fallback and annotate responses with quality tag.
 - Postmortem: gather traces, KV cache hit stats, and quality evals.

[08:56] Ravi Patel: who owns the manual approval? our on-call or redwood SRE?
[09:01] Alex Morgan: typically customer on-call owns approval for KMS changes; Redwood can provide a read-only automated approval path if configured. we recommend a pre-approved DR principal to avoid manual blocks.
[09:12] Lina Gomez: what's the expected end-user impact during failover? latency spikes? degraded quality?
[09:18] Priya Shah: expectation pyramid: 1) small latency increase during warm-up (seconds to minutes), 2) possible quality degradation only if falling back to quantized model, 3) partial feature limits if some storage is region-bound. we quantify these in the worksheet per scenario.
[09:34] Jordan Park: regarding KV cache persistence - do you persist caches to a global store?
[09:38] Daniel Liu: no, KV cache is not global; it's local low-latency memory. persisting would defeat performance. instead we reconstruct via warming and mirror patterns.
[09:48] Emily Chen: about tests - we'd like a benchmark run that simulates failover with 5% of traffic sensitive, and the rest non-sensitive. can redwood run that with us?
[09:57] Priya Shah: yes, we'll draft a benchmark plan. daniel will help with synthetic workloads and expected KPIs.
[10:05] Alex Morgan: ok going to open the floor for any edge questions.
[10:09] Mark Turner: one more - does redwood have region capacity dashboards so we can see available headroom?
[10:15] Sofia Reyes: yes console shows per-region capacity, queued requests, and model-level latency heatmaps. we can provide read-only access to a dashboard for your SREs.
[10:25] Lina Gomez: for the bench, what metrics should we collect?
[10:29] Priya Shah: collect p50/p95/p99 latency, success rate, KV cache hit rate, model quality scores on our prompt set, and egress bytes for cost modeling.
[10:37] Ravi Patel: anything else on encryption? if DR region keys are different, do you surface which key was used per request?
[10:43] Daniel Liu: yes logged per-request key id and region.
[10:47] Jordan Park: regarding canaries - can we do percentage-based rollout and automatic rollback on quality regressions?
[10:53] Priya Shah: yes, Redwood supports percentage rollouts with thresholds; the system can auto-rollback if regression detected on eval metrics.
[10:59] Mark Turner: great. sounds promising. next steps recap please.
[11:03] Alex Morgan: recap: we'll share runbook + pricing worksheet; SE team will send benchmark plan; customer to provide traffic profile and compliance checklist; security to request SOC2/KMS docs. schedule follow-up after bench.
[11:16] Emily Chen: timeline - we need security docs by end of next week for procurement.
[11:20] Alex Morgan: we'll get those to you.
[11:23] Priya Shah: ok closing notes - i'll include the sample synthetic prefixes and the recommended mirroring rates.
[11:28] Mark Turner: thanks everyone.
[11:31] Alex Morgan: thanks; we'll follow up with artifacts and schedule.

End transcript.

Notes: Minor transcription errors are present (e.g., "K V cache" vs "KV cache", "quantizashun" misheard on one segment). Speakers occasionally overlap and some filler words remain.
